content: The human nose is the prominent structure on the face that contains the nostrils. Its shape is primarily determined by the ethmoid bone and the nasal septum, which is largely composed of cartilage and separates the nostrils. Due to the unique vascular anatomy of the nose and its surrounding areas, infections originating in the nasal region can potentially spread retrogradely to the brain. This anatomical vulnerability has led to the designation of the area from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose, including the nose and maxilla, as the danger triangle of the face in medical terminology. Human noses exhibit a wide variety of shapes. Efforts have been made to classify these shapes, such as those described in the 19th-century work Nasology by Eden Warwick (a pseudonym for George Jabet). This text humorously associated nose shapes with personality traits, parodying the pseudoscience of phrenology. Examples of nose classifications include: Class I: The Roman or Aquiline Nose – Characterized by a convex, undulating shape, resembling the curve of an eagle's beak. Class II: The Greek or Straight Nose – Perfectly straight in profile. Class III: The Nubian or Wide-Nostrilled Nose – Broad and thick at the tip, gradually widening from below the bridge, and typically viewed from the front rather than in profile. Class IV: The Hawk Nose – Highly convex, maintaining its curvature like a bow, and thin and sharp in appearance. Class V: The Snub Nose – A short and slightly upturned nose. Class VI: The Turn-Up or Celestial Nose – Featuring a continuous concavity from the eyes to the tip. In Western culture, some individuals undergo rhinoplasty to alter the aesthetic appearance of their nose. Nose piercings, such as those in the nostrils, septum, or bridge, are also common. In New Zealand, the Māori people traditionally greet one another with a nose-pressing gesture called hongi, though this practice is now largely reserved for ceremonial occasions. Several individuals are famously associated with their noses, either due to their distinctive appearance or cultural significance. Examples include: Barbara Streisand – Known for her prominent nose. John Barrymore – Nicknamed The Great Profile for his striking facial features. Cyrano de Bergerac – A historical figure and literary character renowned for his large nose. Adrien Brody – Recognized for his distinctive nose. Tom Cruise – Reportedly declined rhinoplasty early in his career. Jimmy Durante – A comedian whose large nose was a signature feature, humorously exaggerated by cartoonist Al Hirschfeld. Nanette Fabray – Noted for her small nose. Jamie Farr – Portrayed Klinger on MASH, with many jokes about his nose written into the show. Pinocchio – A fictional character whose nose grows when he lies. Bob Hope – Nicknamed ski-nose. Michael Jackson – Known for undergoing multiple nasal surgeries. Major Kovalyov – A character in Nikolai Gogol's novella The Nose. Barry Manilow – Often parodied for his large nose. Al Molinaro – Recognized for his prominent nose in Happy Days. Jack Nicholson – Featured in Chinatown (1974), where his nose plays a notable role in the plot. Richard Nixon – Known for his distinctive nose. Danny Thomas – A comedian with a recognizable nose. The Duke of Wellington – The first Duke was famously nicknamed Nosey by his troops due to his large, hooked nose.
